**Worn Steps**

In old buildings, the stone steps dip in the middle. I find this more moving than most monuments. No one set out to carve that shallow curve. It was made by millions of ordinary footfalls, each removing an amount of stone too small to measure, by people who were thinking about something else entirely: a late appointment, a sick child, lunch.

A monument tells you what someone wanted remembered. A worn step tells you what actually happened. People came this way, again and again, for centuries, and they mostly walked up the center. It is a record with no author and no agenda, which makes it unusually trustworthy.

The same thing shows up everywhere once you start looking. The shiny patch on a bronze statue where tourists rub for luck. The dirt paths that cut across campus lawns, ignoring the paved ones the architects intended. Each is a kind of slow vote, tallied in friction.

What I like most is the scale of it. No single person can wear down granite. You could climb the same staircase every day of your life and leave no visible trace. The curve only exists in aggregate, which means that everyone who contributed did so without knowing. Most of what humans build together works this way: language, cities, customs, recipes. People inherit grooves made by strangers and deepen them slightly for strangers yet to come.

There is some comfort in that. You don't have to leave a mark to be part of the mark.
